cards.body: Your memory fades on a schedule — fast at first, then slower. Psychologists call it the forgetting curve. Spaced repetition beats it by reviewing each fact right before you'd lose it, which flattens the curve a little more every time.
cards.title: Your brain deletes on a schedule

cards.body: Cramming stuffs facts in for tomorrow's test and dumps them by next week. Spacing the exact same reviews across several days builds memories that actually survive. Same effort, wildly different results.
cards.title: Cramming is a scam

cards.body: Day 1: learn it. Day 2: review it (feels hard). Day 4: review it (easier now). Day 8: review it (easy). Every successful recall stretches the next gap a little further.
Miss a flashcard? You'll see it again soon. Nail it three times running? It gets pushed weeks out. The schedule follows your actual memory, not a calendar someone else printed.

choices: It's faster in a single sitting
cards.explain: Spacing triggers the brain's long-term storage machinery. Cramming only parks facts in short-term memory, which empties within days.
cards.q: Why space out reviews instead of cramming?

choices: Fast at first, then more slowly
questions.explain: That's the forgetting curve: a steep early drop that levels off. Spaced reviews interrupt the drop.
questions.q: How does forgetting actually behave over time?

choices: Reviewing just before you'd forget it
Reading the chapter one more time
questions.explain: A well-timed review, when recall takes effort but succeeds, is what strengthens the memory. Effortless re-reading barely registers.
questions.q: Which review timing strengthens memory most?

choices: Push it weeks into the future
questions.explain: A miss means the memory is weak, so the interval shrinks. Easy wins earn longer gaps; struggles earn shorter ones.
questions.q: You blank on a flashcard. What should the schedule do?

choices: Because the gaps force real recall from memory
Because you spend more total hours
questions.explain: The magic isn't more hours — it's that each spaced session forces your brain to reconstruct the memory, which is the workout that builds it.
questions.q: Why does spacing beat one long study session?

choices: An app using spaced repetition, a little daily
One giant cram session the night before
questions.explain: Small, well-timed, effortful recalls compound. Everything else is either too rare or too passive.
questions.q: Which habit actually builds lasting knowledge?

flashcards.back: The pattern of memory fading quickly at first, then more slowly over time.
Scheduling each review just before you'd forget, so every recall strengthens the memory.
It only loads short-term memory, which empties within days without spaced recalls.
flashcards.front: Why does cramming fail in the long run?

flashcards.back: Shorten the interval and see it again soon, until recalling it feels easy.
flashcards.front: You keep missing the same card. What now?

cards.body: Focus is a muscle, and you train it in sprints. The Pomodoro technique: 25 minutes of single-task work, 5 minutes fully off. After four rounds, take a longer break. Knowing focus ends makes starting it far less painful.
cards.title: Focus is a muscle: train it in sprints

cards.body: Re-reading feels productive and mostly isn't. Active recall — closing the book and dragging the answer out of your own head — builds far stronger memory per minute. Effort is the feature, not the bug.
cards.title: Test yourself, don't re-read

cards.body: Try the Feynman check: explain the idea out loud as if teaching a bright 10-year-old. No jargon allowed. Every place you stumble is a precise map of what you don't actually know yet.
Cornell method: notes on the right, key questions on the left, a two-line summary at the bottom. If your notes could have been photocopied from the source, you were transcribing, not learning.

cards.explain: Retrieval practice forces reconstruction, which wires the memory in. Re-reading and highlighting feel fluent but leave almost no trace.
cards.q: Which builds stronger memory per minute?

questions.explain: The classic Pomodoro is 25 on, 5 off — short enough to start, long enough to matter. Four rounds, then a longer break.

choices: Closing the book and recalling the answer
questions.explain: Active recall means retrieving from memory with no cues. The struggle to remember is literally the learning happening.

choices: Exactly what you don't understand yet
questions.explain: The Feynman technique turns explanation gaps into a study plan: wherever you can't say it simply, go re-learn that part.
questions.q: You try explaining a concept simply and get stuck. What did you just find?

choices: Questions and cues on the left, summary at the bottom
A full transcript of the lecture
questions.explain: Cornell notes split the page: notes right, questions left, summary bottom. The questions column becomes your self-quiz later.
questions.q: What makes Cornell notes different from plain notes?

choices: Put the phone away and single-task
Play music with lyrics and multitask
Study in bed to stay relaxed
questions.explain: Focus sprints need one task and zero pings. Lyrics compete with language processing, and beds cue sleep, not study.
questions.q: Which setup makes a Pomodoro actually work?

flashcards.back: 25 minutes of single-task focus followed by a 5-minute break.
Forcing answers out of your own memory instead of re-reading the source.
Learning by explaining an idea in simple terms; where you stumble shows what you don't know.
Key questions and cues — they become your self-quiz later.
